newsitem.title: USA: Fujitsu wants out of chip-plant tax break.
newsitem.headline: Fujitsu wants out of chip-plant tax break.

text.p: Local officials said Thursday they were studying their options after Fujitsu Microelectronics Inc. asked to be released from a deal that obligated it to create new jobs in exchange for a tax break.

The company, a subsidiary of Japanese industrial giant Fujitsu Ltd., had won an agreement from Multnomah County for $23 million in tax concessions for a promised 445 new jobs at a nearly completed $1.3 billion plant in suburban Gresham, Ore.

Because of changing market conditions, the company now plans to mothball its current plant next door and move the entire work force of 630 workers into the new facility, Fujitsu Vice President Dick Romano said.

The decision was based on the collapse of the world market for the 4 megabyte memory chips that the old plant makes and growing demand for the more powerful 64 megabyte chips that the new plant may be the first in the world to mass produce, Romano said.
Dynamic random access memory chips are used in a variety of electronic devices, including personal computers and games.

Multnomah County Commissioner Tanya Collier said lawyers were studying penalty clauses in the contract. She said the purpose of the 15-year concession, under which Fujtsu would have invested $12 million in community service fees and training, child care and housing, was to get unemployed people off welfare and onto career tracks.

Romano said the company has already spent more than $1 million on low-income housing and community-college training courses. He also said he believed the contract was void because the company has not yet received any tax breaks, which do not begin until the plant goes into production.
